Near-Optimal List-Recovery of Linear Code Families

Ray Li ††thanks: Math & CS Department, Santa Clara University. Email: rli6@scu.edu. Research supported by NSF grant CCF-2347371.    Nikhil Shagrithaya ††thanks: Computer Science and Engineering Department, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor. Email: nshagri@umich.edu. Research supported in part by NSF grants CCF-2236931 and CCF-2107345.
Abstract

We prove several results on linear codes achieving list-recovery capacity. We show that random linear codes achieve list-recovery capacity with constant output list size (independent of the alphabet size and length). That is, over alphabets of size at least ℓΩ⁡(1/ε)\ell^{\Omega(1/\varepsilon)}, random linear codes of rate RR are (1−R−ε,ℓ,(ℓ/ε)O⁡(ℓ/ε))(1-R-\varepsilon,\ell,(\ell/\varepsilon)^{O(\ell/\varepsilon)})-list-recoverable for all R∈(0,1)R\in(0,1) and ℓ\ell. Together with a result of Levi, Mosheiff, and Shagrithaya, this implies that randomly punctured Reed–Solomon codes also achieve list-recovery capacity. We also prove that our output list size is near-optimal among all linear codes: all (1−R−ε,ℓ,L)(1-R-\varepsilon,\ell,L)-list-recoverable linear codes must have L≥ℓΩ⁡(R/ε)L\geq\ell^{\Omega(R/\varepsilon)}.

Our simple upper bound combines the Zyablov-Pinsker argument with recent bounds from Kopparty, Ron-Zewi, Saraf, Wootters, and Tamo on the maximum intersection of a “list-recovery ball” and a low-dimensional subspace with large distance. Our lower bound is inspired by a recent lower bound of Chen and Zhang.

1 Introduction

In this work, we study list-recovery for random linear codes and random Reed–Solomon codes, proving near-optimal upper and lower bounds.

An (error correcting) code 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a subset of Σn\Sigma^{n} for an alphabet Σ\Sigma, which, in this work, is always 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} for some prime power qq. We study linear codes, which are subspaces of 𝔽qn\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}. We want codes to be large, meaning they have large rate R=(logq⁡|𝒞|)/nR=\left(\log_{q}|\mathcal{C}|\right)/n. We also want codes to tolerate more errors. In the standard unique decoding setting, tolerating many errors means that, for any vector z∈𝔽qnz\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}, there is at most one codeword c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C} that agrees with zz on many coordinates.

We study a generalization of the unique-decoding problem known as list-recovery. In list-recovery, we want that, for any ℓ×ℓ×⋯×ℓ\ell\times\ell\times\cdots\times\ell combinatorial rectangle, there are few codewords cc that “agree” with this rectangle on many coordinates. Formally, a code 𝒞\mathcal{C} is (ρ,ℓ,L)\left(\rho,\ell,L\right)-list-recoverable if for any sets S1,…,Sn⊂𝔽qS_{1},\dots,S_{n}\subset\mathbb{F}_{q} of size |Si|=ℓ|S_{i}|=\ell, there are at most LL codewords c1,…,cL∈𝒞c_{1},\ldots,c_{L}\in\mathcal{C} such that ci∈Sic_{i}\in S_{i} for at least a (1−ρ)​n(1-\rho)n fraction of the coordinates. The special case of (ρ,1,1)(\rho,1,1) list-recoverability is the standard unique-decoding setting, and the special case of (ρ,1,L)(\rho,1,L) list-recovery is known as list-decoding.

List-recovery has motivations in coding theory, complexity theory, and algorithms. In coding theory, list-recovery has been used as a tool to obtain efficient list-decoding algorithms [GS99, GR08, GW13, Kop15, HRW19]. Also, list-recoverable random-linear codes — which we study in this work — are used as a building block in other coding constructions [GI01, HW18]. In complexity theory, list-recoverable codes find applications in constructions of other pseudorandom objects such as extractors [TZ04] and condensers [GUV09]. In algorithms, they are also useful primitives in group testing [INR10, NPR11] sparse recovery [GNPRS13], and streaming algorithms [LNNT19, DW20].

The list-recovery capacity theorem states that ρ=1−R\rho=1-R is the optimal tradeoff between the error radius ρ\rho and the code rate RR. (see e.g., [GRS19, Res20]). That is, below capacity ρ<1−R\rho<1-R, there exist (p,ℓ,Oℓ​(1))(p,\ell,O_{\ell}(1))-list-recoverable codes of rate RR, and above capacity ρ>1−R\rho>1-R, any (ρ,ℓ,L)(\rho,\ell,L)-list-recoverable code must have exponential list size L≥qΩ⁡(n)L\geq q^{\Omega(n)}. The existence holds because uniformly random codes of rate RR (over sufficiently large alphabets q≥ℓΩ⁡(1/ε)q\geq\ell^{\Omega(1/\varepsilon)}) are (1−R−ε,ℓ,O⁡(ℓ/ε))(1-R-\varepsilon,\ell,O(\ell/\varepsilon))-list-recoverable with high probability.

We wish to understand what kinds of codes achieve list-recovery capacity. A number of explicit code constructions are known to achieve list-recovery capacity, including Folded Reed–Solomon codes, Multiplicity codes, Folded Algebraic–Geometry codes. Additional techniques — subspace evasive sets, subspace designs, and expander techniques — can be used to improve the output list-size LL and alphabet size qq [GR08, Kop15, GW13, GX12, GX13, HW18, HRW19, GK16, DL12, KRSW18, Tam23] (see Table 1 in [KRSW18], see also [Sri24, CZ24] for even tighter list size bounds in the special case of list-decoding).

Still, several fundamental questions remain open.

  1. 1.

    First, how list-recoverable is a random linear code? A random linear code is a random subspace of 𝔽qn\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}. All explicit constructions are based on linear codes (though many are only linear over a subfield), so it is natural to wonder about list-recovery of a “typical” linear code. As list-recovery is a pseudorandom property, this question also addresses the deeper geometric question of “how similar is a random subspace to a random set over 𝔽qn\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}?”, which is well-studied in the more specific context of list-decoding [ZP81, Eli91, GHK11, CGV13, Woo13, RW14, RW15, RW18, LW20, GLMRSW21, AGL24].

  2. 2.

    Second, how list-recoverable are Reed–Solomon codes? The above constructions all generalize the Reed–Solomon code, the most fundamental polynomial evaluation code. Can Reed–Solomon codes themselves achieve list-recovery capacity? Given recent progress that showed the special case that Reed–Solomon codes achieve list-decoding capacity [BGM23, GZ23, AGL24], this general case of list-recovery has been an obvious and tantalizing open question.

  3. 3.

    Lastly, is there a fundamental separation between linear and nonlinear codes for list-recovery? On one hand, there is no apparent separation for the special case of list-decoding, where random linear codes are list-decodable to capacity with list-size O⁡(1/ε)O(1/\varepsilon) [GHK11, Woo13, LW20, GLMRSW21], just like uniformly random codes. On the other hand, uniformly random codes are list-recoverable with list size O⁡(ℓ/ε)O(\ell/\varepsilon), but all known linear constructions require output list size at least ℓΩ⁡(1/ε)\ell^{\Omega(1/\varepsilon)}, and this lower bound has been proven in various specific settings [GLMRSW21, LMS24, CZ24].

We answer all three questions. We show that random linear codes are list-recoverable to capacity with provably near-optimal output list size. By a recent result of [LMS24], this implies that randomly punctured Reed–Solomon codes are list-recoverable to capacity with near-optimal output list size. Lastly, we prove a fundamental separation between linear and non-linear codes by showing that all linear codes of rate RR must have list-size at least L≥ℓΩ⁡(R/ε)L\geq\ell^{\Omega(R/\varepsilon)}.

1.1 Our results

We now state our results in the context of prior work.

1.1.0.0.1 List recovery for Random Linear Codes.

Several known arguments show that random linear codes achieve list-recovery capacity. A random linear code is a code generated by a uniformly random generator matrix 𝐆∈𝔽qn×k\mathbf{G}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n\times k}. First, the Zyablov-Pinsker argument [ZP81] adapted to list-recovery shows that random linear codes of rate RR over alphabet q≥ℓΩ⁡(1/ε)q\geq\ell^{\Omega(1/\varepsilon)} are (1−R−ε,ℓ,qO⁡(ℓ/ε))(1-R-\varepsilon,\ell,q^{O(\ell/\varepsilon)})-list-recoverable (see, for example [Gur04, Lemma 9.6]). Rudra and Wootters [RW18] improved the output list size to qO⁡(log2⁡(ℓ/ε))q^{O(\log^{2}(\ell/\varepsilon))}, showing random linear codes of rate RR over alphabet q≥ℓΩ⁡(1/ε)q\geq\ell^{\Omega(1/\varepsilon)} are (1−R−ε,ℓ,qO⁡(log2⁡(ℓ/ε)))(1-R-\varepsilon,\ell,q^{O(\log^{2}(\ell/\varepsilon))})-list-recoverable. We improve the output list size to be independent of the alphabet size qq.

Theorem 1.1 (Theorem 3.1, Informal).

For all R,ε∈(0,1)R,\varepsilon\in(0,1), and q≥ℓΩ⁡(1/ε)q\geq\ell^{\Omega(1/\varepsilon)} a random linear code of rate RR is (1−R−ε,ℓ,(ℓε)O⁡(ℓ/ε))\left(1-R-\varepsilon,\ell,\left(\frac{\ell}{\varepsilon}\right)^{O(\ell/\varepsilon)}\right)-list-recoverable with high probability.

Our list size improves on the prior bounds when q≥ℓΩ⁡(ℓ/ε)q\geq\ell^{\Omega(\ell/\varepsilon)}, which covers most alphabet sizes (q≥ℓΩ⁡(1/ε)q\geq\ell^{\Omega(1/\varepsilon)} is needed to achieve list-recovery capacity), and the improvement is more significant when qq is larger. This improvement to an alphabet-independent output list size is critical for Theorem 1.2 below (see Remark 1.3). As we show in Theorem 1.5, this output list size is near optimal among all linear codes.

Our proof is simple, combining the Zyablov–Pinsker [ZP81] argument with recent analyses of the list-recovery of explicit constructions like Folded Reed–Solomon codes. In particular, the Zyablov–Pinsker argument [ZP81] shows that a random linear code can be list-recovered so that, with high probability the output list always lies in a subspace of dimension at most O⁡(ℓ/ε)O(\ell/\varepsilon). Naively, this implies an output list size bound of qO⁡(ℓ/ε)q^{O(\ell/\varepsilon)}. However, recent analyses of list-recovering explicit codes [KRSW18, Tam23] showed that subspaces of dimension DD with good distance — random linear codes are well known to have good distance with high probability — can have at most (ℓ/ε)O⁡(D)(\ell/\varepsilon)^{O(D)} points inside an ℓ\ell-list-recovery ball, thus giving our improved output list size. We also show that we get the best possible output list size for our proof technique, in the sense that, for any linear code, there are output lists that span a subspace of dimension at least Ω⁡(ℓ/ε)\Omega(\ell/\varepsilon) (see Proposition 5.2).

1.1.0.0.2 List recovery for Random Reed-Solomon Codes.

Reed–Solomon codes [RS60] are the most fundamental evaluation codes. A Reed–Solomon code is given by nn evaluation points α1,α2,…,αn\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\ldots,\alpha_{n} in a finite field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}, and a degree k<nk<n, and is defined as

RSn,k(α1,…,αn):={(f(α1),…,f(αn))∣f∈𝔽q[x], degf<k}.\text{RS}_{n,k}(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n}):=\left\{\left(f(\alpha_{1}),\ldots,f(\alpha_{n})\right)\mid f\in\mathbb{F}_{q}[x],\text{ }\deg f<k\right\}.

List-decoding and list-recovery of Reed–Solomon codes are well-studied questions. The seminal Guruswami–Sudan [GS99] algorithm showed that Reed–Solomon codes are list-decodable and list-recoverable up to the Johnson radius 1−R​ℓ1-\sqrt{R\ell} [Joh62, GS01]. Since then, there has been much interest in determining whether Reed–Solomon codes are list-decodable and list-recoverable beyond the Johnson bound, and perhaps even up to capacity ρ=1−R\rho=1-R (the capacity is 1−R1-R for both list-decoding and list-recovery). Initially, there was evidence against this possibility [GR06, CW07, BKR10], suggesting that Reed–Solomon codes could not be list-decoded or list-recovered much beyond the Johnson bound. Since then, an exciting line of work has shown, to contrary, that Reed–Solomon codes can beat the Johnson bound for list-decoding [RW14, ST20, FKS22, GST22, GLSTW22, BGM23, GZ23, AGL24], and, in fact, can be list-decoded up to capacity [BGM23, GZ23, AGL24]. All of these works studied randomly punctured Reed–Solomon codes, where α1,…,αn\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{n} are chosen at random from a larger field qq.

Despite the exciting progress for list-decoding, there has been comparatively little progress on list-recovery. Lund and Potukuchi [LP20] and Guo, Li, Shanggaun, Tamo, and Wootters [GLSTW22] proved that (randomly punctured) Reed–Solomon codes are list-recoverable beyond the Johnson bound in the low-rate regime: [LP20] shows (ρ,ℓ,L)(\rho,\ell,L)-list-recovery for ρ≤1−1/2\rho\leq 1-1/\sqrt{2}, L=O⁡(ℓ)L=O(\ell) and rate O⁡(1ℓ​log⁡q)O\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\ell}\log q}\right), and [GLSTW22] shows (Ω⁡(εℓ​log⁡(1/ε)),ℓ,O⁡(ℓ/ε))\left(\Omega\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{\ell}\log(1/\varepsilon)}\right),\ell,O(\ell/\varepsilon)\right)-list-recovery for rate 1−ε1-\varepsilon Reed–Solomon codes. Both improve on the Johnson radius of O⁡(1ℓ)O\left(\frac{1}{\ell}\right) in the low rate setting.

In [LMS24], Levi, Mosheiff and Shagrithaya showed that random Reed–Solomon codes and random linear codes are locally equivalent, meaning that both random code families achieve identical rate thresholds for all “local properties,” which include (the complements of) list-decoding and list-recovery. Thus, our result for list-recovery of random linear codes transfers to random RS codes as well.

Theorem 1.2 (Theorem 4.1, Informal).

For all R,ε∈(0,1)R,\varepsilon\in(0,1), a randomly punctured Reed–Solomon code of length nn over alphabet size q=n⋅(ℓ/ε)(ℓ/ε)O⁡(ℓ/ε)q=n\cdot(\ell/\varepsilon)^{(\ell/\varepsilon)^{O(\ell/\varepsilon)}}, of rate RR is (1−R−ε,ℓ,(ℓε)O⁡(ℓ/ε))\left(1-R-\varepsilon,\ell,\left(\frac{\ell}{\varepsilon}\right)^{O(\ell/\varepsilon)}\right)-list-recoverable with high probability.

Remark 1.3.

We note that in order to use the equivalence result from [LMS24], it is crucial that the upper bound on the list size be independent of the alphabet size, as guaranteed by Theorem 1.1. Hence, previous results on list size cannot be used with the equivalence result.

Remark 1.4.

A fruitful line of work [GR08, Kop15, GW13, DL12, KRSW18, Tam23] has culminated in output list sizes of O​(ℓε)O⁡(log⁡(ℓ)/ε)O\left(\frac{\ell}{\varepsilon}\right)^{O(\log(\ell)/\varepsilon)} for various explicit list-recoverable codes such as Folded Reed–Solomon codes and Multiplicity codes. This list size is better than our list size of (ℓε)O⁡(ℓ/ε)(\frac{\ell}{\varepsilon})^{O(\ell/\varepsilon)} by roughly a factor of ℓ/log⁡(ℓ)\ell/\log(\ell) in the exponent. However, our results are still interesting because, as described above, the list-recovery of random linear codes and Reed–Solomon codes are fundamental questions, and also because our results yield linear codes for list-recovery and use much smaller alphabet sizes.

1.1.0.0.3 Lower bounds for list-recovery.

We now discuss impossibility results for list-recovery. An early impossibility result of Guruswami and Rudra in [GR06] showed that, in the setting of zero-error list-recovery (ρ=0\rho=0), many full length Reed–Solomon codes of rate RR require R≤1/ℓR\leq 1/\ell in order to have polyn\poly n output list size, so many full length Reed–Solomon codes cannot be list-recovered beyond the Johnson bound — note this does not contradict Theorem 1.2, as we consider randomly punctured, as opposed to full length (n=qn=q) codes. More recently it was shown that achieving list-recovery capacity requires exponential list size ℓΩ⁡(1/ε)\ell^{\Omega(1/\varepsilon)} for particular codes: random linear codes in the high-rate zero-error (ρ=0\rho=0) regime [GLMRSW21], random linear codes in general parameter settings [LMS24], and for Reed–Solomon codes, Folded Reed–Solomon codes, and Multiplicity codes in general parameter settings [CZ24].

Inspired by the lower bound in [CZ24], we show that any linear code list-recoverable to capacity must have output list size at least ℓΩ⁡(R/ε)\ell^{\Omega(R/\varepsilon)}.

Theorem 1.5 (Theorem 5.1, Informal).

Over any field, any linear code of rate RR that is (1−R−ε,ℓ,L)(1-R-\varepsilon,\ell,L) list-recoverable must satisfy L≥ℓΩ⁡(R/ε)L\geq\ell^{\Omega(R/\varepsilon)}.

One takeaway from Theorem 1.5 is that our list sizes of (ℓ/ε)O⁡(ℓ/ε)(\ell/\varepsilon)^{O(\ell/\varepsilon)} in Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.2 are near-optimal. Additionally, Doron and Wootters [DW20] asked whether there were explicit list-recoverable codes with, among other desired guarantees, output list size L=O⁡(ℓ)L=O(\ell). Our result shows this is not possible with any linear code. Lastly, our lower bound shows separation between non-linear and linear codes for list-recovery, which is perhaps surprising given that no such separation exists for list-decoding.

We point out that, for list-decoding (ℓ=1\ell=1), our lower bound is trivial (L≥1L\geq 1), so it does not contradict the recent results that random linear codes, randomly punctured Reed–Solomon codes, and randomly punctured Algebraic-Geometry codes achieve list-decoding capacity with output list size O⁡(1/ε)O(1/\varepsilon) [BGM23, GZ23, AGL24, BDG+23].

2 Preliminaries

For a prime power qq, let 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} be the finite field of order qq. Let [n][n] denote the set {1,…,n}\left\{1,\ldots,n\right\}. For a given vector space VV, let ℒ⁡(V)\mathcal{L}(V) denote the set of all subspaces of VV. For a given set SS, let 2S2^{S} denote the power set of SS. For a vector vv, let v⁡[i]v[i] denote its iith entry.

A code 𝒞⊆𝔽qn\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} is said to be linear if it is a linear subspace, and said to have rate R∈(0,1)R\in(0,1) if R=d​i​m​(𝒞)/nR=dim(\mathcal{C})/n. We say 𝒞\mathcal{C} has relative distance δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) if ∀c∈𝒞,w​t​(c)≥δ⋅n\forall c\in\mathcal{C},wt(c)\geq\delta\cdot n, where w​t​(c)wt(c) denotes the number of non-zero entries in the codeword cc. A matrix 𝐆∈𝔽qn×R​n\mathbf{G}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n\times Rn} containing linearly independent columns is said to be the generator matrix of 𝒞\mathcal{C} if every codeword c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C} can be constructed using some linear combinations of the columns in 𝐆\mathbf{G}. 𝒞\mathcal{C} is said to contain a set of vectors s1,…​sb∈𝔽qns_{1},\ldots s_{b}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} if si∈𝒞s_{i}\in\mathcal{C} for every i∈[b]i\in[b].

For a vector x∈𝔽qnx\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} and sets S1,…,Sn⊆𝔽qS_{1},\ldots,S_{n}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}, the agreement set agr⁡(x,S1,…,Sn)\agr(x,S_{1},\ldots,S_{n}) is defined as:

agr⁡(x,S1,…,Sn)≔{i∈[n]∣x⁡[i]∈Si}.\agr(x,S_{1},\ldots,S_{n})\coloneqq\left\{i\in[n]\mid x[i]\in S_{i}\right\}.

A ρ\rho-radius ℓ\ell-list-recovery ball B(ρ,S1×⋯×Sn)B(\rho,S_{1}\times\cdots\times S_{n}) is given by input lists S1,…,Sn⊆𝔽qS_{1},\dots,S_{n}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q} of size ℓ\ell, and is defined to be

B(ρ,S1×⋯×Sn)={x∈𝔽qn:agr(x,S1×⋯×Sn)≥(1−ρ)n}.\displaystyle B(\rho,S_{1}\times\cdots\times S_{n})=\left\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}:\agr(x,S_{1}\times\dots\times S_{n})\geq(1-\rho)n\right\}. (1)

We can alternatively define (ρ,ℓ,L)(\rho,\ell,L)-list-recovery using the above definition: a code 𝒞⊆𝔽qn\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} is (ρ,ℓ,L)(\rho,\ell,L)-list-recoverable if every ρ\rho-radius ℓ\ell-list-recovery ball BB contains at most LL codewords.

For 0<R<10<R<1, a random linear code (RLC) of rate RR is a linear code whose generator matrix 𝐆∈𝔽qn×R​n\mathbf{G}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n\times Rn} is a matrix whose entries are chosen uniformly at random from 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}, independently of one another. For α1,…,αn∈𝔽q\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}, we use 𝖱𝖲⁡(α1,…,αn,R​n)\mathsf{RS}\left(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n};Rn\right) to denote the Reed–Solomon (RS) code of rate RR obtained by evaluating polynomials of degree <R​n<Rn on evaluation points α1,…,αn∈𝔽q\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}. We say this is a random RS code if the evaluation points have been chosen uniformly at random and independently of one another11 1 This is different from the usual model for random RS codes, where it is required that the random evaluation points be distinct. However, it can be shown that both models behave similarly (refer to [LMS24], Appendix A for details)..

2.1 Local Coordinate-Wise Linear (LCL) Properties

We now introduce the machinery in [LMS24] that connects random linear codes to (randomly punctured) Reed–Solomon codes. A code property 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} for codes of block length nn in 𝔽qn\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} is simply a family of codes in 𝔽qn\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}. We say that a code 𝒞n⊆𝔽qn\mathcal{C}_{n}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} satisfies 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} if 𝒞n∈𝒫n\mathcal{C}_{n}\in\mathcal{P}_{n}. Denoting 𝒫≔{𝒫n}n∈ℕ\mathcal{P}\coloneqq\left\{\mathcal{P}_{n}\right\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}, we say that an infinite family of codes 𝒞n≔{𝒞n}n∈ℕ\mathcal{C}_{n}\coloneqq\left\{\mathcal{C}_{n}\right\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} satisfies 𝒫\mathcal{P} if 𝒞n∈𝒫n\mathcal{C}_{n}\in\mathcal{P}_{n} for every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. In this paper, we focus on local, monotone-increasing code properties. A local code property, informally speaking, is defined by the inclusion of some bad set. A monotone-increasing code property is one for which the following is true: if 𝒞\mathcal{C} satisfies 𝒫\mathcal{P}, then every 𝒞′\mathcal{C}^{\prime} for which 𝒞′⊇𝒞\mathcal{C}^{\prime}\supseteq\mathcal{C} holds, also satisfies 𝒫\mathcal{P}. An example of local, monotone-increasing code property is the complement of (ρ,L)(\rho,L)-list-decodability, defined as the family of all codes that contain at least one set of L+1L+1 distinct vectors, all lying within a Hamming ball of radius ρ\rho.

For a locality parameter b∈ℕb\in\mathbb{N}, an ordered tuple of subspaces 𝒱=(𝒱1,…,𝒱n)\mathcal{V}=(\mathcal{V}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{V}_{n}), where 𝒱i∈𝔽qb\mathcal{V}_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{b} for each i∈[n]i\in[n] is defined to be a bb-local profile. Note that 𝒱∈ℒ​(𝔽qb)n\mathcal{V}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{F}_{q}^{b})^{n}. We say that a matrix A∈𝔽qn×bA\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n\times b} is contained in 𝒱\mathcal{V} if the iith row of A belongs to 𝒱i\mathcal{V}_{i}, for all ii. A code 𝒞⊆𝔽qn\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} is said to contain 𝒱\mathcal{V} if there exists a matrix A∈𝔽qn×bA\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n\times b} with distinct columns such that the set of columns of AA is contained in 𝒞\mathcal{C}, and moreover, AA is contained in 𝒱\mathcal{V}. For a family of bb-local profiles {ℱn}n∈ℕ\left\{\mathcal{F}_{n}\right\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}, where ℱn⊆ℒ​(𝔽qb)n\mathcal{F}_{n}\subseteq\mathcal{L}\left(\mathbb{F}_{q}^{b}\right)^{n}, we define a bb-local coordinate wise linear (bb-LCL) property 𝒫≔{𝒫n}n∈ℕ\mathcal{P}\coloneqq\left\{\mathcal{P}_{n}\right\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} as follows:

𝒫n={𝒞∈𝔽qn∣∃𝒱∈ℱn​ such that ​𝒞​ contains ​𝒱}.\mathcal{P}_{n}=\left\{\mathcal{C}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}\mid\exists\mathcal{V}\in\mathcal{F}_{n}\textrm{ such that }\mathcal{C}\textrm{ contains }\mathcal{V}\right\}.

The complement of (ρ,ℓ,L)(\rho,\ell,L)-list-recoverability is a (L+1)(L+1)-LCL property. This is proven in [LMS24, Proposition 2.2], but we provide a justification in this paragraph. Every bad set of vectors lying within a given ρ\rho-radius ℓ\ell-list-recovery ball agrees with some input lists S1,…,Sn⊆𝔽qS_{1},\ldots,S_{n}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q} at a lot of coordinates. This implies that the vectors agree with one another at a lot of coordinates as well, and once we arrange the bad vector sets as rows in a matrix of dimension n×(L+1)n\times(L+1), we can specify these agreements as linear constraints on the rows of such matrices. Formally, the property is defined by a family of (L+1)(L+1)-local profiles that we now describe. For every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, we define ℱn\mathcal{F}_{n} by describing the (L+1)(L+1)-local profiles 𝒱∈ℒ​(𝔽qL+1)n\mathcal{V}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{F}_{q}^{L+1})^{n} that constitute it. Let S(1−ρ)⊆(2[n])L+1S_{(1-\rho)}\subseteq\left(2^{[n]}\right)^{L+1} denote the collection of all L+1L+1-length tuples where each element is a subset of [n][n] of size exactly (1−ρ)​n(1-\rho)n. Furthermore, let M[ℓ]≔[ℓ]n×(L+1)M_{[\ell]}\coloneqq[\ell]^{n\times(L+1)} denote the set of all matrices of dimension n×(L+1)n\times(L+1) having elements in [ℓ][\ell] 22 2 Even though S(1−ρ)S_{(1-\rho)} and M[ℓ]M_{[\ell]} depend on nn, we have suppressed this dependence in the notation for sake of clarity.. Then, for every s=(s1,…,s(L+1))∈S(1−ρ)s=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{(L+1)})\in S_{(1-\rho)}, every M∈M[ℓ]M\in M_{[\ell]}, define 𝒱⁡(s,M)=(𝒱1,…,𝒱n)\mathcal{V}(s,M)=(\mathcal{V}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{V}_{n}) such that for every i∈[n]i\in[n],

𝒱i≔{r∈𝔽qL+1∣∀j,k∈[L+1],r[j]=r[k] if (i∈sj)∧(i∈sk)∧(M[i,j]=M[i,k])}.\mathcal{V}_{i}\coloneqq\left\{r\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{L+1}\mid\forall j,k\in[L+1],r[j]=r[k]\textrm{ if }(i\in s_{j})\land(i\in s_{k})\land(M[i,j]=M[i,k])\right\}.

Note that each 𝒱i\mathcal{V}_{i} is a subspace of 𝔽q(L+1)\mathbb{F}_{q}^{(L+1)}, and therefore 𝒱⁡(s,M)\mathcal{V}(s,M) is a valid linear profile. We can now define the associated family of linear profiles for the complement of (ρ,ℓ,L)(\rho,\ell,L)-list-recoverability:

ℱn≔{𝒱∈ℒ(𝔽qL+1)n∣∃s∈S(1−ρ),M∈M[ℓ], such that 𝒱=𝒱(s,M)}.\mathcal{F}_{n}\coloneqq\left\{\mathcal{V}\in\mathcal{L}\left(\mathbb{F}_{q}^{L+1}\right)^{n}\mid\exists s\in S_{(1-\rho)},M\in M_{[\ell]},~\textrm{ such that }\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{V}(s,M)\right\}.

Observe that

|ℱ𝒫|≤|S(1−ρ)|⋅|M[ℓ]|≤(nρ​n)(L+1)⋅ℓ(L+1)​n.\left|\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{P}}\right|\leq\left|S_{(1-\rho)}\right|\cdot\left|M_{[\ell]}\right|\leq\binom{n}{\rho n}^{(L+1)}\cdot\ell^{(L+1)n}. (2)

In the same work, the authors also prove a threshold theorem for random linear codes (RLCs) in relation to all LCL properties, and moreover, gave a complete characterization of the rate threshold. Informally, the theorem says that RLCs of a sufficiently large alphabet exhibit a sharp threshold phenomenon for all LCL properties, that is, for every LCL property 𝒫\mathcal{P}, there exists a rate threshold R𝒫R_{\mathcal{P}} such that RLCs of rate R𝒫−εR_{\mathcal{P}}-\varepsilon satisfy 𝒫\mathcal{P} with high probability, and RLCs of rate R𝒫+εR_{\mathcal{P}}+\varepsilon do not satisfy 𝒫\mathcal{P} with high probability.

Theorem 2.1 ([LMS24], Theorem 3.1).

Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be a bb-LCL property of codes in 𝔽qn\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} and let ℱ⊆ℒ​(𝔽qb)n\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{L}\left(\mathbb{F}_{q}^{b}\right)^{n} be a corresponding family of profiles. Let 𝒞⊆𝔽qn\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} be an RLC of rate R. Then, there is some threshold rate R𝒫R_{\mathcal{P}} for which the following holds.

  1. 1.

    If R≥R𝒫+εR\geq R_{\mathcal{P}}+\varepsilon then 𝐏𝐫[𝒞​ satisfies ​𝒫]≥1−q−ε​n+b2\mathop{\bf Pr\/}[\mathcal{C}\textrm{ satisfies }\mathcal{P}]\geq 1-q^{-\varepsilon n+b^{2}}.

  2. 2.

    If R≤R𝒫−εR\leq R_{\mathcal{P}}-\varepsilon then 𝐏𝐫[𝒞​ satisfies ​𝒫]≤|ℱ|⋅q−ε​n+b2\mathop{\bf Pr\/}[\mathcal{C}\textrm{ satisfies }\mathcal{P}]\leq\left|\mathcal{F}\right|\cdot q^{-\varepsilon n+b^{2}}.

  3. 3.

    In particular, if R≤R𝒫−εR\leq R_{\mathcal{P}}-\varepsilon and q≥22​log2​|ℱ|ε​nq\geq 2^{\frac{2\log_{2}|\mathcal{F}|}{\varepsilon n}} then 𝐏𝐫[𝒞​ satisfies ​𝒫]≤q−ε​n2+b2\mathop{\bf Pr\/}[\mathcal{C}\textrm{ satisfies }\mathcal{P}]\leq q^{-\frac{\varepsilon n}{2}+b^{2}}.

The concept of LCL properties allows for “transfer type” theorems between random linear codes and random RS codes. In more detail, for every reasonable LCL property (that is, for every LCL property whose corresponding family of profiles is large), the rate thresholds for random linear codes and random RS codes are the same. That is, any rate threshold proved for LCL properties of RLCs also applies for random RS codes, and vice versa. For our purposes, we only require one part of this result, which we formally state below.

Theorem 2.2 ([LMS24], Theorem 3.10 (part 1) (Threshold theorem for RS codes)).

Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be a bb-LCL property of codes in 𝔽qn\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}, with associated local profile family ℱ𝒫⊆ℒ​(𝔽qb)n\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{P}}\subseteq\mathcal{L}\left(\mathbb{F}_{q}^{b}\right)^{n} and (random linear code) threshold rate R𝒫R_{\mathcal{P}}. Let 0<R′<10<R^{\prime}<1 and let 𝒞=𝖱𝖲𝔽q​(α1,…,αn,R′​n)\mathcal{C}=\mathsf{RS}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}\left(\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{n};R^{\prime}n\right), and α1,…,αn\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{n} are sampled independently and uniformly from 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. Assume that q>R′​n​bq>R^{\prime}nb. Fix ε′​n≥2​b​(b+1)\varepsilon^{\prime}n\geq 2b(b+1). If R′≤R𝒫−ε′R^{\prime}\leq R_{\mathcal{P}}-\varepsilon^{\prime}, then

𝐏𝐫[𝒞​ satisfies ​𝒫]≤(2b−1)⋅((4​b)4​b​R′​nε′​q)ε′​n2​b⋅|ℱ𝒫|.\mathop{\bf Pr\/}[\mathcal{C}\textrm{ satisfies }\mathcal{P}]\leq(2^{b}-1)\cdot\left(\frac{(4b)^{4b}R^{\prime}n}{\varepsilon^{\prime}q}\right)^{\frac{\varepsilon^{\prime}n}{2b}}\cdot|\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{P}}|. (3)

3 List-recovery of Random Linear Codes

In this section, we prove Theorem 1.1, that random linear codes achieve list-recovery capacity with constant output list size. Formally, we show the following.

Theorem 3.1.

Fix 0<R<10<R<1, ε>0\varepsilon>0 so that (1−R−ε)>0(1-R-\varepsilon)>0, ℓ∈ℕ\ell\in\mathbb{N}, and let qq be a prime power such that q≥max⁡(ℓ8​Rε+6,ℓ⋅24/ε)q\geq\max\left(\ell^{\frac{8R}{\varepsilon}+6},\ell\cdot 2^{4/\varepsilon}\right). Let 𝒞⊆𝔽qn\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} be an RLC of rate RR. Then with probability at least 1−2​q−ε​n81-2q^{-\frac{\varepsilon n}{8}}, 𝒞\mathcal{C} is ((1−R−ε),ℓ,L)\left((1-R-\varepsilon),\ell,L\right)-list-recoverable with LL satisfying L≤(2​ℓε)2​ℓ/εL\leq\left(\frac{2\ell}{\varepsilon}\right)^{2\ell/\varepsilon}.

The theorem follows as a consequence of two lemmas. We first state both lemmas, and then give the proof of Theorem 3.1 using them. The first lemma essentially states that any low dimensional subspace with good distance has few points in a list-recovery ball. This lemma appears in [KRSW18, Tam23]; we state the version from [Tam23, Lemma 3.1].

Lemma 3.2 ([Tam23], see also [KRSW18]).

For ε>0\varepsilon>0 and ℓ∈ℕ\ell\in\mathbb{N}, let 𝒞⊆𝔽qn\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} be a linear code with relative distance δ>ε/2\delta>\varepsilon/2 that is (δ−ε2,ℓ,L)(\delta-\frac{\varepsilon}{2},\ell,L)-list-recoverable. Assume further that any output list is contained in a subspace V⊆𝒞V\subseteq\mathcal{C} of dimension rr. Then the output list size L≤(2​ℓε)rL\leq\left(\frac{2\ell}{\varepsilon}\right)^{r}.

The second lemma uses the Zyablov–Pinsker argument [ZP81], showing that a random linear code does not have too many linearly independent codewords within a list-recovery ball.

Lemma 3.3.

Fix 0<R<10<R<1, ε>0\varepsilon>0 so that (1−R−ε)>0(1-R-\varepsilon)>0, ℓ∈ℕ\ell\in\mathbb{N}, and let qq be a prime power such that q≥max⁡(ℓ8​Rε+6,ℓ⋅24/ε)q\geq\max\left(\ell^{\frac{8R}{\varepsilon}+6},\ell\cdot 2^{4/\varepsilon}\right). Let 𝒞⊆𝔽qn\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} be an RLC of rate RR. Then with probability at least 1−q−ε​n​L81-q^{-\frac{\varepsilon nL}{8}}, for every input lists 𝒮1,…,𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{S}_{n} of size ℓ\ell, the maximal linearly independent subset of 𝒞\mathcal{C} within the (1−R−ε)(1-R-\varepsilon) radius ℓ\ell-list-recovery ball B((1−R−ε),S1×⋯×Sn)B\left((1-R-\varepsilon),S_{1}\times\cdots\times S_{n}\right) has size less than 2​ℓ/ε2\ell/\varepsilon.

Proof of Lemma 3.3.

Denote ρ:=1−R−ε\rho:=1-R-\varepsilon and L:=2​ℓ/εL:=2\ell/\varepsilon. We also assume qq is a multiple of ℓ\ell for simplicity of exposition, and note that the result holds in the general case as well. We show that an RLC “avoids” all bad configurations with high probability. A bad configuration is a set VV of linearly independent vectors of size LL such that there exist input lists lists 𝒮1,…,𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{S}_{n} of size ℓ\ell, so that V⊆B(ρ,S1×⋯×Sn)V\subseteq B\left(\rho,S_{1}\times\cdots\times S_{n}\right). We say that 𝒞\mathcal{C} contains a bad configuration VV if for every v∈Vv\in V, vv is also in 𝒞\mathcal{C}. If this condition is not satisfied, then we say that 𝒞\mathcal{C} does not contain VV. It is easy to see that if 𝒞\mathcal{C} contains no bad configurations, then the maximal linearly independent subset of 𝒞\mathcal{C} within any ℓ\ell-list-recovery ball of radius ρ\rho has size less than 2​ℓ/ε2\ell/\varepsilon. Therefore we show that the probability of 𝒞\mathcal{C} containing a bad configuration is low.

Fix input lists 𝒮1,…,𝒮n\mathcal{S}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{S}_{n} of size ℓ\ell, and let B:=B(ρ,S1×⋯×Sn)B:=B\left(\rho,S_{1}\times\cdots\times S_{n}\right) be the corresponding ρ\rho radius ℓ\ell-list-recovery ball. The size of BB is (nρ​n)⋅ℓ(1−ρ)​n⋅(q−ℓ)ρ​n\binom{n}{\rho n}\cdot\ell^{(1-\rho)n}\cdot(q-\ell)^{\rho n}. The probability that a particular configuration is bad is equal to the probability of the encodings of some LL linearly independent messages being inside BB simultaneously, which is (|B|qn)L\left(\frac{|B|}{q^{n}}\right)^{L}. By a union bound over at most qn​ℓq^{n\ell} possible input lists and all LL-sized linearly independent subsets of the message vectors in 𝔽qR​n\mathbb{F}_{q}^{Rn} (there are at most qR​n​Lq^{RnL} such subsets), we have

𝐏𝐫𝒞[𝒞​ contains a bad configuration]\displaystyle\mathop{\bf Pr\/}_{\mathcal{C}}[\mathcal{C}\text{ contains a bad configuration}] ≤((nρ​n)⋅ℓ(1−ρ)​n⋅(q−ℓ)ρ​nqn)L⋅qn​ℓ⋅qR​n​L\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{\binom{n}{\rho n}\cdot\ell^{(1-\rho)n}\cdot(q-\ell)^{\rho n}}{q^{n}}\right)^{L}\cdot q^{n\ell}\cdot q^{RnL}
=((ℓq)n⋅(nρ​n)⋅(qℓ−1)ρ​n)L⋅qn​ℓ⋅qR​n​L\displaystyle=\left(\left(\frac{\ell}{q}\right)^{n}\cdot\binom{n}{\rho n}\cdot\left(\frac{q}{\ell}-1\right)^{\rho n}\right)^{L}\cdot q^{n\ell}\cdot q^{RnL}
≤((ℓq)n⋅(q/ℓ)Hq/ℓ​(ρ)​n)L⋅qn​ℓ⋅qR​n​L\displaystyle\leq\left(\left(\frac{\ell}{q}\right)^{n}\cdot(q/\ell)^{H_{q/\ell}(\rho)n}\right)^{L}\cdot q^{n\ell}\cdot q^{RnL}
≤((q/ℓ)−(1−Hq/ℓ​(ρ))​n)L⋅qn​ℓ⋅qR​n​L\displaystyle\leq\left((q/\ell)^{-(1-H_{q/\ell}(\rho))n}\right)^{L}\cdot q^{n\ell}\cdot q^{RnL}
≤((q/ℓ)−(R+3​ε4)​n)L⋅qn​ℓ⋅qR​n​L\displaystyle\leq\left((q/\ell)^{-\left(R+\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}\right)n}\right)^{L}\cdot q^{n\ell}\cdot q^{RnL} (4)
=ℓ(R+3​ε4)​n​L⋅q−(R+3​ε4)​n​L⋅qε​n​L2⋅qR​n​L\displaystyle=\ell^{(R+\frac{3\varepsilon}{4})nL}\cdot q^{-\left(R+\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}\right)nL}\cdot q^{\frac{\varepsilon nL}{2}}\cdot q^{RnL}
=ℓ(R+3​ε4)​n​L⋅q−ε​n​L4\displaystyle=\ell^{(R+\frac{3\varepsilon}{4})nL}\cdot q^{-\frac{\varepsilon nL}{4}}
≤q−ε​n​L8.\displaystyle\leq q^{-\frac{\varepsilon nL}{8}}.

In Equation 4, we used q≥ℓ⋅24/εq\geq\ell\cdot 2^{4/\varepsilon}, and for the last inequality, we used q≥ℓ8​Rε+6q\geq\ell^{\frac{8R}{\varepsilon}+6}. This implies that the probability with which 𝒞\mathcal{C} does not contain any bad configuration is at least 1−q−ε​n​L81-q^{-\frac{\varepsilon nL}{8}}. ∎

We now prove Theorem 3.1.

Proof of Theorem 3.1.

Denote ρ:=1−R−ε\rho:=1-R-\varepsilon. Denote by E1E_{1} the event that for a RLC 𝒞\mathcal{C} of rate RR, the maximal linearly independent subset of 𝒞\mathcal{C} within every (1−R−ε)(1-R-\varepsilon) radius ℓ\ell-list-recovery ball has size less than 2​ℓ/ε2\ell/\varepsilon. By Lemma 3.3, we know that E1E_{1} happens with probability at least 1−q−ε​n​L81-q^{-\frac{\varepsilon nL}{8}}. Let E2E_{2} denote the event that a rate RR RLC 𝒞\mathcal{C} has distance at least 1−R−ε21-R-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}. By the Gilbert-Varshamov bound (see [GRS22], Section 4.2), and because of the fact that q≥ℓ⋅24/ε≥24/εq\geq\ell\cdot 2^{4/\varepsilon}\geq 2^{4/\varepsilon}, E2E_{2} happens with probability at least 1−q−ε​n21-q^{-\frac{\varepsilon n}{2}}. Therefore we have

𝐏𝐫𝒞[E1∧E2]≥1−q−ε​n​L8−q−ε​n2≥1−2⋅q−ε​n8\mathop{\bf Pr\/}_{\mathcal{C}}[E_{1}\land E_{2}]\geq 1-q^{-\frac{\varepsilon nL}{8}}-q^{-\frac{\varepsilon n}{2}}\geq 1-2\cdot q^{-\frac{\varepsilon n}{8}}

When E1E_{1} and E2E_{2} occur simultaneously, the assumptions of Lemma 3.2 are satisfied by 𝒞\mathcal{C} with r=2​ℓ/εr=2\ell/\varepsilon and δ=1−R−ε2\delta=1-R-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}, and therefore we see that

𝐏𝐫𝒞[⋀B|𝒞∩B|≤(2​ℓε)2​ℓ/ε]≥1−2⋅q−ε​n8\mathop{\bf Pr\/}_{\mathcal{C}}\left[\bigwedge_{B}\left|\mathcal{C}\cap B\right|\leq\left(\frac{2\ell}{\varepsilon}\right)^{2\ell/\varepsilon}\right]\geq 1-2\cdot q^{-\frac{\varepsilon n}{8}}

where BB is ranging over all (1−R−ε)(1-R-\varepsilon) radius ℓ\ell-list-recovery balls, and we are done. ∎

4 List-Recovery of Reed–Solomon codes

In this section, we will prove the following result, which says that random Reed–Solomon codes are list-recoverable to capacity with constant output list size. The proof combines Theorem 3.1 from the previous section with Theorem 2.1, the equivalence theorem from [LMS24].

Corollary 4.1.

Fix 0<R<10<R<1, ε>0\varepsilon>0 so that (1−R−ε)>0(1-R-\varepsilon)>0, ℓ∈ℕ\ell\in\mathbb{N}. Fix a constant ε′>0\varepsilon^{\prime}>0 such that ε′<R\varepsilon^{\prime}<R, and denote L≔⌊(2​ℓε)2​ℓ/ε⌋L\coloneqq\lfloor{\left(\frac{2\ell}{\varepsilon}\right)^{2\ell/\varepsilon}}\rfloor. Let η>0\eta>0 be a constant, and let qq be a prime power satisfying q>(4​(L+1))4​(L+1)​R​nε′⋅2((log⁡ℓ+2)​(L+1)+η)⋅2​(L+1)ε′q>\frac{(4(L+1))^{4(L+1)}Rn}{\varepsilon^{\prime}}\cdot 2^{\frac{((\log\ell+2)(L+1)+\eta)\cdot 2(L+1)}{\varepsilon^{\prime}}}. Then, a random RS code of rate R−ε′R-\varepsilon^{\prime} over 𝔽qn\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} is (1−R−ε,ℓ,L)(1-R-\varepsilon,\ell,L)-list-recoverable with probability at least 1−2−η​n1-2^{-\eta n}.

Proof of Corollary 4.1.

Denote L≔⌊(2​ℓε)2​ℓ/ε⌋L\coloneqq\lfloor{\left(\frac{2\ell}{\varepsilon}\right)^{2\ell/\varepsilon}}\rfloor and b≔L+1b\coloneqq L+1. Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be the bb-LCL property of not being (1−R−ε,ℓ,L)(1-R-\varepsilon,\ell,L)-list-recoverable, and let R𝒫R_{\mathcal{P}} be the corresponding (random linear code) threshold rate. By Theorem 2.1, part 1 [LMS24], we know that if 𝒞\mathcal{C} is an RLC of rate RR, then the following holds for every constant ε∗>0\varepsilon^{*}>0:

𝐏𝐫[𝒞​ satisfies ​𝒫]<1−qε∗​n+b2⟹R<R𝒫+ε∗\mathop{\bf Pr\/}[\mathcal{C}\textrm{ satisfies }\mathcal{P}]<1-q^{\varepsilon^{*}n+b^{2}}\implies R<R_{\mathcal{P}}+\varepsilon^{*}

According to Theorem 3.1, a rate RR RLC (having a sufficiently large alphabet size) satisfies 𝒫\mathcal{P} only with probability at most 2​q−ε​n8<1−qε∗​n+b22q^{-\frac{\varepsilon n}{8}}<1-q^{\varepsilon^{*}n+b^{2}}. Therefore, R<R𝒫+ε∗R<R_{\mathcal{P}}+\varepsilon^{*} for every ε∗>0\varepsilon^{*}>0, and so R≤R𝒫R\leq R_{\mathcal{P}}.

We will now work with random RS codes having rate slightly less than RR. Define R′≔R−ε′≤R𝒫−ε′R^{\prime}\coloneqq R-\varepsilon^{\prime}\leq R_{\mathcal{P}}-\varepsilon^{\prime}, take nn to be large enough so that ε′​n≥2​b​(b+1)\varepsilon^{\prime}n\geq 2b(b+1). Note that q>R​n​b>R′​n​bq>Rnb>R^{\prime}nb. Define 𝒞=𝖱𝖲𝔽q​(α1,…,αn,R′​n)\mathcal{C}=\mathsf{RS}_{\mathbb{F}_{q}}\left(\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{n};R^{\prime}n\right), where α1,…,αn\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{n} are sampled independently and uniformly from 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. Upon denoting ℱ𝒫\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{P}} to be the local profile family associated with property 𝒫\mathcal{P}, we see that the hypothesis of Theorem 2.2 [LMS24] is satisfied, and therefore, Equation 3 is satisfied.

Recall that we calculated an upper bound for |ℱ𝒫|\left|\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{P}}\right| in Equation 2, and so |ℱ𝒫|≤(n(1−R−ε)​n)b⋅ℓb​n\left|\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{P}}\right|\leq\binom{n}{(1-R-\varepsilon)n}^{b}\cdot\ell^{bn}. Substituting this bound on |ℱ𝒫|\left|\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{P}}\right| in Equation 3,

𝐏𝐫[𝒞​ satisfies ​𝒫]\displaystyle\mathop{\bf Pr\/}[\mathcal{C}\textrm{ satisfies }\mathcal{P}] ≤(2b−1)⋅((4​b)4​b​R′​nε′​q)ε′​n2​b⋅|ℱ𝒫|\displaystyle\leq(2^{b}-1)\cdot\left(\frac{(4b)^{4b}R^{\prime}n}{\varepsilon^{\prime}q}\right)^{\frac{\varepsilon^{\prime}n}{2b}}\cdot|\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{P}}|
≤((4​b)4​b​R′​nε′​q)ε′​n2​b⋅(n(1−R−ε)​n)b⋅ℓb​n\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{(4b)^{4b}R^{\prime}n}{\varepsilon^{\prime}q}\right)^{\frac{\varepsilon^{\prime}n}{2b}}\cdot\binom{n}{(1-R-\varepsilon)n}^{b}\cdot\ell^{bn}
≤((4​(L+1))4​(L+1)​R′​nε′​q)ε′​n2​(L+1)⋅2(H2​(1−R−ε)+1)⋅(L+1)​n.\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{(4(L+1))^{4(L+1)}R^{\prime}n}{\varepsilon^{\prime}q}\right)^{\frac{\varepsilon^{\prime}n}{2(L+1)}}\cdot 2^{(H_{2}(1-R-\varepsilon)+1)\cdot(L+1)n}.

Because q>(4​(L+1))4​(L+1)​R′​nε′⋅2((log⁡ℓ+2)​(L+1)+η)⋅2​(L+1)ε′q>\frac{(4(L+1))^{4(L+1)}R^{\prime}n}{\varepsilon^{\prime}}\cdot 2^{\frac{((\log\ell+2)(L+1)+\eta)\cdot 2(L+1)}{\varepsilon^{\prime}}}, we see that 𝐏𝐫[𝒞​ satisfies ​𝒫]≤2−η​n\mathop{\bf Pr\/}[\mathcal{C}\textrm{ satisfies }\mathcal{P}]\leq 2^{-\eta n}. Thus, 𝒞\mathcal{C} is (1−R−ε,ℓ,L)(1-R-\varepsilon,\ell,L)-list-recoverable with probability at least 1−2−η​n1-2^{-\eta n}. ∎

5 Any linear code needs output list-size ℓΩ⁡(R/ϵ)\ell^{\Omega(R/\epsilon)}

We now prove our lower bounds for list-recovery, that any linear code list-recoverable to capacity needs output list size ℓΩ⁡(R/ε)\ell^{\Omega(R/\varepsilon)}.

Theorem 5.1.

Let R,ε∈(0,1)R,\varepsilon\in(0,1), ℓ\ell be a positive integer, and n≥n0​(ℓ,R,ε)n\geq n_{0}(\ell,R,\varepsilon) be sufficiently large. Let 𝒞⊆𝔽n\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathbb{F}^{n} be a linear code of rate RR. If 𝒞\mathcal{C} is (1−R−ε,ℓ,L)(1-R-\varepsilon,\ell,L)-list-recoverable, then L>ℓ⌊R/ε⌋L>\ell^{\lfloor{R/\varepsilon}\rfloor}.

Proof.

Let k≔R​nk\coloneqq Rn be the dimension of the code. Let k′=⌈εR⋅k⌉k^{\prime}=\left\lceil{\frac{\varepsilon}{R}\cdot k}\right\rceil. Let m=⌊k−1k′+1⌋m=\left\lfloor{\frac{k-1}{k^{\prime}+1}}\right\rfloor. By Gaussian elimination and permuting rows and columns, we may, without loss of generality write the generator matrix of 𝒞\mathcal{C} as

𝐆=[11⋱⋱1∗∗⋯⋯∗]\displaystyle\mathbf{G}=\begin{bmatrix}1&&&&\\ &1&&&\\ &&\ddots&&\\ &&&\ddots&\\ &&&&1\\ \hline\cr*&*&\cdots&\cdots&*\\ \end{bmatrix} (5)

where each ∗* is a length n−kn-k vector. For i∈[k]i\in[k], let vi∈𝔽nv_{i}\in\mathbb{F}^{n} denote the columns. By rank-nullity, there exist vectors w0,…,wm−1∈𝔽nw_{0},\dots,w_{m-1}\in\mathbb{F}^{n} such that wiw_{i} is a linear combination of vi⋅(k′+1)+1,…,v(i+1)⋅(k′+1)v_{i\cdot(k^{\prime}+1)+1},\dots,v_{(i+1)\cdot(k^{\prime}+1)} such that wiw_{i} is not supported on indices k+1,…,k+k′k+1,\dots,k+k^{\prime} (there are k′+1k^{\prime}+1 vectors and k′k^{\prime} indices). Now let wm=vkw_{m}=v_{k}. Restricted to indices in [k+k′][k+k^{\prime}], vectors w0,…,wmw_{0},\dots,w_{m} have pairwise disjoint supports: within indices [k+k′][k+k^{\prime}], for i=0,…,m−1i=0,\dots,m-1, vector wiw_{i} is supported on i⋅(k′+1)+1,…,(i+1)⋅(k′+1)≤k−1i\cdot(k^{\prime}+1)+1,\dots,(i+1)\cdot(k^{\prime}+1)\leq k-1, and vector wmw_{m} is supported on k,…,k+k′k,\dots,k+k^{\prime}.

Now fix ℓ\ell arbitrary distinct values β1,…,βℓ∈𝔽q\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{\ell}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}. Consider the output list ℒ={∑i=0mβri​wi:ri∈[ℓ]}\mathcal{L}=\{\sum_{i=0}^{m}\beta_{r_{i}}w_{i}:r_{i}\in[\ell]\} to be all linear combinations of wiw_{i} with coefficients from β1,…,βℓ\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{\ell}. The fact that the vectors w0,…,wmw_{0},\dots,w_{m} have pairwise disjoint supports on [k+k′][k+k^{\prime}] implies (i) the vectors w0,…,wmw_{0},\dots,w_{m} are linearly independent, and so all vectors in ℒ\mathcal{L} are distinct, and (ii) the vectors in ℒ\mathcal{L} can only take on one of ℓ\ell values at any index in [k+k′][k+k^{\prime}]. Therefore, we can choose input lists S1,…,Sk+k′S_{1},\dots,S_{k+k^{\prime}}, each of size ℓ\ell such that all codewords in ℒ\mathcal{L} agree with all of S1,…,Sk+k′S_{1},\dots,S_{k+k^{\prime}}.

Choosing the rest of the input lists arbitrarily, we have that this code is not (ρ,ℓ,L)(\rho,\ell,L) list-recoverable with radius ρ=(n−k−k′)/n<1−R−ε\rho=(n-k-k^{\prime})/n<1-R-\varepsilon and list size L=ℓm+1≥ℓ⌊R/ε⌋.L=\ell^{m+1}\geq\ell^{\lfloor{R/\varepsilon}\rfloor}.33 3 m+1=⌊k+k′k′+1⌋≥⌊k+εR​kεR​k+2⌋≥⌊Rε⌋m+1=\left\lfloor{\frac{k+k^{\prime}}{k^{\prime}+1}}\right\rfloor\geq\left\lfloor{\frac{k+\frac{\varepsilon}{R}k}{\frac{\varepsilon}{R}k+2}}\right\rfloor\geq\left\lfloor{\frac{R}{\varepsilon}}\right\rfloor, where we used that k>2​R2/ε2k>2R^{2}/\varepsilon^{2}.

∎

We also show that our Zyablov-Pinsker type argument in Theorem 1.1 (Lemma 3.3) is tight, in the sense that any linear code must have Ω⁡(ℓ/ε)\Omega(\ell/\varepsilon) linearly independent codewords in a list-recovery ball.

Proposition 5.2.

Let R,ε∈(0,1)R,\varepsilon\in(0,1), ℓ\ell be a positive integer, and n≥n0​(ℓ,R,ε)n\geq n_{0}(\ell,R,\varepsilon) be sufficiently large. Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a linear code of rate RR. Then there exists a (1−R−ε)(1-R-\varepsilon) radius ℓ\ell-list-recovery ball BB that contains at least ⌈(1−R)​ℓ/ε⌉−1\lceil{(1-R)\ell/\varepsilon}\rceil-1 linearly independent elements of 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

Proof.

Upon writing the generator matrix of 𝒞\mathcal{C} in the same form as described above in the proof of Theorem 5.1, consider the first m≔⌈(1−R)​ℓ/ε⌉−1<(1−R)​ℓ/εm\coloneqq\lceil{(1-R)\ell/\varepsilon}\rceil-1<(1-R)\ell/\varepsilon columns of the generator matrix. Denote these linearly independent column vectors by v1,…,vmv_{1},\ldots,v_{m}. Create input lists S1,…,SkS_{1},\dots,S_{k} each of size ℓ\ell that contain 00 and 11, but are otherwise arbitrary. Then create lists Sk+1,…,SnS_{k+1},\dots,S_{n} of size ℓ\ell, each containing elements that are evenly distributed so that they agree equally with each of v1,…,vmv_{1},\dots,v_{m}. Thus, each of v1,…,vmv_{1},\dots,v_{m} agrees with S1,…,SnS_{1},\dots,S_{n} on the first kk, and on at least ⌊ℓm⋅(n−k)⌋>ε​n\lfloor{\frac{\ell}{m}\cdot(n-k)}\rfloor>\varepsilon n of the remaining coordinates. Therefore, these vectors lie inside a (1−R−ε)​n(1-R-\varepsilon)n-radius ℓ\ell-list-recovery ball around S1,…,SnS_{1},\dots,S_{n}, as desired. ∎

6 Concluding remarks

We showed that random linear codes and Reed–Solomon codes are list-recoverable to capacity with near-optimal output-list size. Several open questions remain.

  1. 1.

    What is the optimal output-list size for random linear codes and Reed–Solomon codes? There is a gap between our upper bound of (ℓε)O⁡(ℓ/ε)(\frac{\ell}{\varepsilon})^{O(\ell/\varepsilon)} and the lower bound of ℓΩ⁡(1/ε)\ell^{\Omega(1/\varepsilon)}. We surmise that the correct answer is closer to the lower bound.

  2. 2.

    As asked by Doron and Wootters [DW20], are there explicit list-recoverable codes with output list size L=Oε​(ℓ)L=O_{\varepsilon}(\ell)? (and, even better, over alphabet size q=poly(ℓ)q=\poly(\ell)). We showed (Theorem 1.5) that any such code must be nonlinear.

  3. 3.

    Our alphabet size for list-recovering Reed–Solomon codes (Theorem 1.2) is optimal in that it is linear in nn, but the constant is double-exponential in ℓ/ε\ell/\varepsilon. By contrast, for list-decoding, the best known alphabet size for achieving capacity has an exponential-type constant, 2poly(1/ε)⋅n2^{\poly(1/\varepsilon)}\cdot n [AGL24]. Can our alphabet size be improved?

7 Acknowledgments

The authors would like to thank Yeyuan Chen and Zihan Zhang for pointing out a mistake in Theorem 5.1 in an earlier version of the paper.
